ideas.title: 60,000 New Cases This Year. Here Is What That Number Means.
ideas.brief: Lead with the ACS figure of approximately 60,480 projected new oral cavity and oropharyngeal cancer cases in the US. Each slide breaks down one dimension of the number: who is most affected, how many are caught late, and what a two-minute screener can change. Close with a direct prompt to take the free risk screener at oralcheck.org.

ideas.title: Only Smokers Get Oral Cancer. That Is Not True Anymore.
ideas.brief: Open with the myth stated plainly, then dismantle it slide by slide: HPV is now the leading cause of oropharyngeal cancer in adults under 50, and cases are rising in people who have never used tobacco. Keep the tone informative rather than alarming, and end with a nudge to check personal risk at oralcheck.org.

ideas.title: HPV Can Cause Oral Cancer. Most People Have No Idea.
ideas.brief: Frame the post around the awareness gap: HPV is widely known as a cervical-cancer risk, but its role in oropharyngeal cancer is still largely unknown to the public, and the fastest-growing patient group is adults aged 35 to 55. Walk through what HPV-linked oral cancer looks like, who it affects, and why early detection is the single biggest factor in survival. End with oralcheck.org.

ideas.title: How to Check Your Own Mouth for Early Warning Signs
ideas.brief: A step-by-step visual guide to a 60-second at-home oral self-exam: what to look for (white or red patches, sores that do not heal within two weeks, lumps, difficulty swallowing), how to position a mirror, and what to do if something looks off. Tone is calm and practical, never frightening. Final slide points to oralcheck.org for a deeper risk assessment.

ideas.title: Ten Questions. Two Minutes. Free. That Is the Screener.
ideas.brief: A single, clean image post built around the low-effort, high-value message: the OralCheck screener takes about two minutes, costs nothing, and gives people a concrete sense of their personal risk. Copy leans on specificity (two minutes, no account) rather than generic health urgency. The caption closes with a direct link to oralcheck.org.

ideas.title: Oral Cancer Lives Under the Head and Neck Umbrella
ideas.brief: Timed to World Head and Neck Cancer Day on July 27, this infographic maps where oral cancer sits within the broader head and neck cancer family, names the other cancers in that group, and explains why early detection is the shared survival lever across all of them. Include a short list of warning signs common to the category. Caption closes with oralcheck.org.

ideas.title: What Survival Rates Actually Look Like by Stage
ideas.brief: Use the documented contrast in outcomes between early-stage and late-stage oral cancer to make the case for screening without sensationalism. The overall five-year survival rate sits around 69%, but that number shifts dramatically depending on when the cancer is found. Each slide presents one stage and what detection at that point typically means for treatment. End with oralcheck.org as the logical next step.

ideas.title: Your Dentist Appointment Just Did More Than You Realized
ideas.brief: A warm, relatable post that reframes the routine dental visit as a quiet line of defense against oral cancer, without leaning into fear. The tone is gently observational: most people sit in that chair thinking about their next cleaning, not realizing a trained eye is also scanning for early signs of something more serious. Caption ends with an encouragement to go further at oralcheck.org.

ideas.title: The Head and Neck Cancer Umbrella Most People Have Never Heard Of
ideas.brief: World Head and Neck Cancer Day (July 27) is a chance to show followers where oral cancer sits within the broader head and neck category, which also includes throat, thyroid, and salivary gland cancers. Slide 1 opens with the stat that head and neck cancers account for nearly 4% of all U.S. cancers, then each slide names one site in plain language, closes on why early detection across all these sites is the factor that most determines outcome. Final slide directs to the free screener.

ideas.title: July 27 Is One Day. Early Detection Is Every Day.
ideas.brief: A World Head and Neck Cancer Day tie-in that keeps the focus narrow and actionable: one day on the calendar is a prompt, but the screener at oralcheck.org is available 365 days a year. The copy leads with the awareness day date, explains that two minutes is all it takes, and frames the screener as the practical thing anyone can do right now to mark the occasion.

ideas.title: Tour de France Riders Cover More Miles Than Most People Know About Oral Cancer
ideas.brief: The Tour de France covers roughly 3,400 kilometers over 21 stages, a number most cycling fans know by heart. Fewer people know that about 60,480 Americans are projected to be diagnosed with oral cancer in 2026, a figure that has climbed steadily for a decade. The post pairs both numbers to make the point that we track athletic endurance with precision but miss a cancer whose survival rate jumps dramatically when it's caught early.

ideas.title: What Happens Inside Your Mouth When HPV Goes Undetected
ideas.brief: Most people associate HPV with cervical cancer, not the mouth. This carousel closes that gap: Slide 1 opens on the fact that oropharyngeal cancer rates have risen sharply in adults 35 to 55 while tobacco-related oral cancers have declined, Slide 2 explains how HPV-related oral cancers often develop at the back of the throat where a home mirror check won't catch them, Slide 3 explains what a clinical screening adds that a self-exam alone cannot, and the final slide points to oralcheck.org as a first step toward knowing personal risk.

ideas.title: Five Things Your Dentist Checks That Have Nothing to Do With Teeth
ideas.brief: Framed from the dentist's perspective rather than the patient's, this carousel walks through five non-tooth findings a trained clinician looks for during a routine exam: lymph node size and firmness, the floor of the mouth, the soft palate, the lateral tongue borders, and the oropharynx. Each slide is one finding, one plain-language explanation, and one thing the reader can ask their provider about. The angle is that a twice-yearly dental visit is already a partial cancer screening, most patients just don't realize it.

ideas.title: The Symptom People Ignore for Months Because It Seems Minor
ideas.brief: Research consistently shows that a significant share of oral cancer patients waited more than 90 days from first noticing a symptom to seeking care, often because the sore, patch, or lump seemed like it would resolve on its own. The carousel opens on that delay finding, then walks through four symptoms that commonly get dismissed (a sore that doesn't heal in three weeks, a white or red patch, unexplained numbness, a lump in the neck), and closes with a plain-language explanation of why earlier presentation changes outcomes. Points to oralcheck.org.

ideas.title: Oral Cancer Rates Are Rising in People Who Have Never Touched a Cigarette
ideas.brief: This post does not revisit the smoker-only myth directly (already posted) but approaches it from the data trend angle: incidence in never-smokers under 50 has grown while incidence in heavy smokers has declined, driven by HPV prevalence. The infographic shows two diverging trend lines in plain, visual terms and lands on the key takeaway that lifestyle assumptions are not a reliable proxy for risk. Ends with the oralcheck.org screener prompt.

ideas.title: Brushing Twice a Day and Still Missing a Two-Minute Check That Matters
ideas.brief: A warm, relatable post that starts from a universal truth: most people have a thorough tooth-brushing routine they never skip but have never once done a structured oral cancer self-check in the same two minutes. The tone is gently knowing, not guilt-inducing. The copy acknowledges that the self-check isn't something anyone teaches you, normalizes not knowing, and then offers oralcheck.org as the easy next step. Flagged for manual review per light_lane protocol.

ideas.title: Seven in Ten HPV-Aware Adults Still Miss the Oral Cancer Link
ideas.brief: A new JAMA Oncology study found that 70.8% of people who already know about HPV still don't know it can cause oral cancer. The reel opens on that stat as a visual hook, then walks through the simple knowledge gap: HPV is widely associated with cervical cancer but its role in throat and mouth cancers is barely discussed. Closes with the screener CTA at oralcheck.org.

ideas.title: Men and Oral HPV: the Risk Doesn't Peak and Then Stop
ideas.brief: Bust the assumption that HPV risk is a young-adult issue that fades after your twenties. A 2025 study published in Cancer found men face substantial lifelong risk of acquiring oral HPV, making this a myth that cuts across age groups. Slides move from the myth ('you're past the risky years') to the reality, then to what regular screening actually catches.

ideas.title: Back to School Means Annual Physicals. Add One More Check.
ideas.brief: Late summer's back-to-school season drives a surge in routine health appointments. Tie that cultural moment to a simple reminder: an oral cancer screening takes about two minutes and is often skipped even during a full checkup. A clean, warm visual of someone at a routine appointment with copy that connects the familiar back-to-school ritual to this one overlooked step. Ends with oralcheck.org.

ideas.title: About 7 Percent of Adults Have Oral HPV Right Now
ideas.brief: CDC data shows roughly 7% of people carry oral or oropharyngeal HPV at any given time, with no symptoms and no way to know without screening. The carousel visualizes what 7% looks like in a crowd, then explains why most carriers never find out, and what to do if you want to understand your own risk level. Ends with the screener at oralcheck.org.

ideas.title: A Sore That's Been There Three Weeks Deserves a Second Look
ideas.brief: Most people dismiss a mouth sore as a minor irritation, and most of the time they're right. But a sore that doesn't heal within two to three weeks is one of the clearest early warning signs of oral cancer, and the delay between noticing it and acting on it is where outcomes diverge sharply. Slides walk through the specific signs that cross the line from 'wait and see' to 'get this checked,' framed as a practical decision guide rather than a scare piece.

ideas.title: The Wimbledon Final Fills One Court. Oral Cancer Fills Far More Seats.
ideas.brief: Wimbledon 2025 just wrapped, and Centre Court holds about 14,979 people. The reel uses that familiar image of a packed, electric crowd and points out that roughly 59,660 Americans will be diagnosed with oral or oropharyngeal cancer this year, filling Centre Court nearly four times over. The comparison makes an abstract annual number feel immediate and real without sensationalizing it. The reel closes on early detection as the stat that changes the outcome, with oralcheck.org.

ideas.title: What Your Mouth Is Actually Telling You After Years of Good Habits
ideas.brief: A warm, slightly wry take aimed at the health-conscious person who tracks their steps, eats well, and still hasn't thought about oral cancer risk, because it doesn't feel like it belongs in their category of worry. The copy acknowledges the irony gently: good habits matter and they don't make you immune. The tone is curious and empathetic, never preachy. Ends with a nudge to take the two-minute screener at oralcheck.org. This goes to manual review per light_lane protocol.

ideas.title: HPV-16 Shows Up in Nine Out of Ten Oropharyngeal Cancers in Men
ideas.brief: HPV-16, a single strain of the virus, is found in approximately 90% of oropharyngeal cancer cases in men in the United States, according to recent research. Most men have never heard this number. The carousel unpacks what oropharyngeal means in plain language (the back of the throat, base of the tongue, tonsils), why one strain drives such a large share of cases, and what early detection actually looks like for this type of cancer. Closes with oralcheck.org.

ideas.title: Head and Neck Cancer Month. Most People Still Miss This Part.
ideas.brief: Recovered from run 32056316958 logs after the ledger push was rejected.

ideas.title: Alcohol Is an Oral Cancer Risk Factor Most People Never Hear About
ideas.brief: Tied to National Recovery Month (September 1), this carousel surfaces alcohol as one of the three primary modifiable risk factors for oral cancer, a fact most people in recovery conversations never encounter. A 2026 Lancet Americas study found that alcohol use may raise susceptibility to oral high-risk HPV infection, giving the post a fresh, peer-reviewed hook that goes beyond the familiar tobacco framing. Each slide moves from the risk finding to the concrete action: take the free screener at oralcheck.org.

ideas.title: 58,500 Diagnoses a Year. Most People Can't Picture That Number.
ideas.brief: Open with the 2026 figure of roughly 58,500 Americans diagnosed with oral or pharyngeal cancer this year, then give it scale through a striking, sourced comparison, such as the capacity of a sold-out NFL stadium (roughly 65,000 seats) or the population of a recognizable mid-size U.S. city, so the number stops being abstract. Each slide pairs the visual comparison with a plain-language fact about early detection, ending on the screener CTA. The comparison must be chosen so it is clearly tasteful and not trivializing of the disease.

ideas.title: Three Minutes on a Sunday Can Actually Tell You Something Real
ideas.brief: A warm, human carousel that walks through the small, unhurried Sunday-morning ritual of a quick oral self-check, framed around the kind of self-care people already do on a slow morning (checking the mirror, making coffee) rather than around fear or urgency. Each slide covers one thing to look for, in plain, friendly language, with the final slide noting that if anything looks off after three weeks, the next step is a conversation with a clinician, and that oralcheck.org is a free, no-account starting point. This idea goes to manual review before publishing.

ideas.title: Even Moderate Drinking May Raise Your Oral HPV Risk
ideas.brief: September is National Recovery Month, and a 2026 Lancet Americas study finding that even modest alcohol use may increase susceptibility to high-risk oral HPV gives OralCheck a specific, peer-reviewed hook. The carousel opens with the Recovery Month context, walks through how alcohol, HPV, and oral cancer connect in a clear chain, and closes with the free screener at oralcheck.org as the low-friction next step. Tone is factual and non-judgmental: this is about information, not shame.

ideas.title: Dental Hygiene Month Is About More Than Clean Teeth
ideas.brief: National Dental Hygiene Month is the right moment to surface what hygienists already do at every visit: check for unusual patches, sores, and lumps that can be early signs of oral cancer. The carousel walks through what a professional oral cancer screening at a dental visit actually covers, then shows what a self-exam between visits looks like, slide by slide. It ends with the reminder that oralcheck.org is a free way to assess personal risk before the next appointment.

ideas.title: Your Mouth Keeps a Better Diary Than You Do
ideas.brief: A warm, gently witty carousel that reframes the oral self-exam as paying attention to something your body has been quietly tracking all along. Each slide names one thing worth noticing, a sore that hasn't moved in three weeks, a patch that wasn't there last month, a spot that feels different, framed as 'things your mouth has been meaning to tell you.' The final slide grounds it with the fact that most oral cancers found early are treatable, and points to oralcheck.org for a free risk check. Goes to manual review.

ideas.title: Stoptober Starts October 1. Your Mouth Has a Stake in It.
ideas.brief: Stoptober, the NHS-backed 28-day quit-smoking challenge beginning October 1, gives OralCheck a timely, credible hook to connect tobacco to oral cancer risk on a day when millions are already talking about quitting. The reel opens with a single on-screen stat — tobacco remains one of the three primary modifiable risk factors for oral cancer — then moves through a calm, plain-spoken voiceover explaining that quitting is the single biggest lifestyle change a person can make for their oral health. It closes by inviting viewers to take the free screener at oralcheck.org while that quit-smoking energy is already top of mind.

ideas.title: Recovery Month and the Alcohol Risk Most People Skip
ideas.brief: September is National Recovery Month, when alcohol and substance-use conversations dominate health media at scale — and a 2026 Lancet Americas paper found that even modest alcohol consumption may raise susceptibility to high-risk oral HPV infection, giving this post a specific, peer-reviewed finding to stand on. The reel draws a grounding comparison: the number of Americans diagnosed with oral cancer each year is roughly equal to the full capacity of a sold-out NFL stadium, and alcohol is one of the least-discussed risk factors in that count. Voiceover stays factual and non-stigmatising, framing the screener at oralcheck.org as a two-minute step anyone can take this month, whatever their relationship with alcohol looks like.

ideas.title: Your Dental Hygienist Sees Something Your Mirror Might Miss
ideas.brief: National Dental Hygiene Month is the natural moment to reframe the routine cleaning appointment as a whole-mouth health check, not just a plaque removal session — and this reel does that with warmth rather than alarm. Shot-list style: a person settling into a dental chair, a hygienist moving methodically through a soft-tissue exam, a close-up of someone rinsing and leaving with an easy smile. The voiceover notes that a hygienist checks tissue, gums, and the floor of the mouth at every visit — and that between appointments, a quick self-check at home, paired with the free screener at oralcheck.org, keeps that continuity going.

ideas.title: 13,150 Deaths This Year. Most Were Findable Early.
ideas.brief: The ACS projects 13,150 oral cancer deaths in the US in 2026. That number is the population of a small American town, which gives the audience a human-scale image rather than an abstract figure. The post contrasts that death toll with the well-documented survival advantage of early detection, then directs followers to take the free screener at oralcheck.org. Photo query: 'aerial view small town main street'.

ideas.title: What to Actually Ask Your Hygienist This October
ideas.brief: National Dental Hygiene Month is the brief, and the angle is the patient as an active participant: most people sit back and let the hygienist lead, but a single direct question ('can you look for any unusual patches or sores?') turns a routine clean into a two-minute oral cancer screen. The post frames that one question as the most productive thing a person can do in October, then points to oralcheck.org for a risk check between appointments. Photo query: 'patient talking to dental hygienist chair'.

ideas.title: You Don't Have to Smoke or Have HPV to Raise Your Risk
ideas.brief: The myth to bust is the binary people carry: oral cancer comes from either tobacco or HPV, full stop. A 2026 Lancet Americas paper found that even modest alcohol use may increase susceptibility to high-risk oral HPV, which means routine social drinking can quietly compound risk in people who consider themselves low-risk on both counts. The post names that gap plainly, without alarm, and closes by directing followers to take the free screener at oralcheck.org. Photo query: 'person declining drink at social gathering'.

ideas.title: Follow along: what a dental oral cancer check covers
ideas.hook: Your dentist checks six things at every visit. Can you find them first?
ideas.brief: Each shot prompts the viewer to look at one area in their own mouth, lips, gums, tongue, cheeks, palate, throat, in the same order a dentist would. After the self-check, a single title card notes that most early oral cancers are found during routine dental visits, and that people who skip that care tend to reach diagnosis at later stages when outcomes are worse. The reel closes with a prompt to take a free risk screener at oralcheck.org/learn/prevention.

ideas.title: HPV overtook tobacco as the top throat cancer cause
ideas.hook: Tobacco is not the leading cause of throat cancer anymore.
ideas.brief: The correction lands first: tobacco has been overtaken by HPV as the primary driver of oropharyngeal cancers, meaning the tonsils, base of tongue and back of the throat. The supporting figure follows: cases have risen by more than 300% since the 1980s. A final line holds the nuance in place, noting that tobacco remains the biggest driver of cancers in the mouth itself, so this shift is specific to the throat. Photo shows a candid mid-adult couple, hinting at the demographic without alarm. Caption closes with oralcheck.org/learn/hpv.

ideas.title: A biopsy turns a white patch into an answer
ideas.hook: You notice a white patch. You wait. It is still there.
ideas.brief: Slide 1 states the myth: if a clinician looks at it and says nothing urgent, it must be fine. Slide 2 takes it apart: no one, not a clinician and not a photograph, can tell a harmless patch from a dangerous one by eye alone. Slide 3 names what actually gives an answer: a small tissue sample taken under local anaesthetic and examined under a microscope, a short appointment, not a procedure to dread. Final slide: oralcheck.org/learn/white-and-red-patches.

ideas.title: Six HPV throat cancer symptoms worth knowing
ideas.hook: Six symptoms can point toward HPV-related throat cancer.
ideas.brief: The hook names the count, then the caption lists all six in plain language: a sore throat that hasn't resolved in two weeks, a painless neck lump, food that feels like it's catching, one-sided ear pain without an ear infection, hoarseness lasting more than two weeks, and unexplained weight loss. A closing sentence notes that none of these is proof of anything, but any one persisting beyond two weeks is worth getting checked. Photo shows a person touching their neck or throat, candid and unposed. Caption closes with oralcheck.org/learn/hpv.

ideas.title: The two-week rule for a sore in your mouth
ideas.hook: Most mouth sores heal on their own within two weeks.
ideas.brief: Slide 1 describes what a canker sore looks like: round or oval, white or yellow center, red rim, painful, appearing only inside the mouth. Slide 2 marks the window: 7 to 14 days is the normal healing time. Slide 3 covers what does not follow that pattern: a lesion that is often painless early, has irregular or raised or hard edges, may bleed when touched, and is still there on day 15. Final slide: day 15 is when the sore gets checked, at oralcheck.org/learn/canker-sore-vs-oral-cancer.

ideas.title: Painless patches: the warning sign that feels like nothing
ideas.hook: No pain, no problem. That logic does not apply here.
ideas.brief: Open on the contrast: pain is what most people wait for, but early oral cancer frequently does not hurt. Cut to a close shot of the inner cheek, then the tongue, showing where red and white patches appear and noting both can be completely painless. Close with the two-week rule: if a patch is still there after two weeks, that absence of pain is not reassurance. Check it at oralcheck.org/learn/signs.

ideas.title: Lower lip sun exposure risk: what outdoor workers should know
ideas.hook: Press your lower lip forward and take a close look.
ideas.brief: Start with the instruction: pull the lower lip out and look at its outer surface, the part that faces the sun. Explain that chronic sun exposure is a leading risk factor specifically for lower lip cancer, and that people who work outdoors are at higher risk than those who do not. Close on the two practical steps that offer meaningful protection: SPF lip balm and a wide-brimmed hat. Learn more at oralcheck.org/learn/prevention.

ideas.title: The floor of your mouth is the hardest spot to self-check
ideas.hook: Lift your tongue to the roof of your mouth right now.
ideas.brief: The instruction opens the post and doubles as the self-exam itself. The caption explains what the viewer is looking at: the U-shaped tissue under the tongue, one of the highest-risk sites in the mouth, and one that can hide a small tumor for months before causing any discomfort. The closing line reinforces that the only way to see it is this exact move, which is why most people have never looked. Photo shows a person using a small mirror to examine the inside of their mouth. Caption closes with oralcheck.org/learn/signs.

ideas.title: How to check the sides of your tongue right now
ideas.hook: Stick your tongue out as far as it will go.
ideas.brief: Slide 1 gives the instruction: tongue out, then turn it gently to look at the left side, then the right, then lift it to see the underside. Slide 2 names why this spot matters: the sides and underside of the tongue are the most common site for oral cancer overall, and they are the easiest to miss without deliberately looking. Slide 3 closes with a single action: if anything looks or feels different after this check, log it at oralcheck.org/learn/signs.

ideas.title: Men diagnosed with oral cancer 2.6 times more than women
ideas.hook: 2.6 times. That's how much more often men are diagnosed.
ideas.brief: The figure opens without ceremony, then the caption gives it context: SEER age-adjusted incidence shows men are diagnosed with oral cancer roughly 2.6 times as often as women. A second sentence adds the layer that HPV-related throat cancer most often affects men between 40 and 60, which means the risk isn't concentrated only in older age groups. The post does not moralize; it names the disparity and leaves room for the viewer to act on it. Photo shows a man in his forties or fifties at a routine health checkup. Caption closes with oralcheck.org/learn/facts.

ideas.title: What two weeks tells you about a mouth sore
ideas.hook: You notice a sore spot on your cheek. It's day three.
ideas.brief: The carousel opens on that moment: a small irritation, easy to dismiss. Slide by slide, it walks through what the two-week window actually means: cold sores, minor abrasions, and irritation from a sharp tooth or food burn typically resolve within 14 days. The final slides shift the frame: if something is still there on day 15, that is not a reason to panic, but it is a reason to have it looked at. A note grounds the whole piece: tobacco is the single biggest modifiable risk factor for oral cancer, and quitting measurably lowers that risk, even years later. Closes with a prompt to take the free screener at oralcheck.org/learn/prevention.

ideas.title: Painless neck lump as a first sign of HPV throat cancer
ideas.hook: Have you felt a lump in your neck that just will not go away?
ideas.brief: Open with the question aimed at the viewer's own experience, then explain that a painless swollen node in the neck is often the first sign of HPV-related throat cancer, caused by lymph node involvement. Show the location: the sides of the neck, just below the jaw. Land on the threshold that matters: a lump that persists for more than two weeks without an obvious infection is worth getting checked. More at oralcheck.org/learn/hpv.

ideas.title: When Gum Disease Is Not Gum Disease
ideas.hook: Gum disease and gum cancer can look nearly identical.
ideas.brief: Open on a close shot of healthy gum tissue, narrating what normal color, texture, and firmness look like. Cut to the same area showing redness, swelling, or a thickened patch, and explain that these changes are shared by both gum disease and early gum cancer. Land on the one clue that separates them: a tooth that has come loose without any dental explanation, which is worth reporting to a clinician rather than waiting out. Close with the screen oralcheck.org/learn/signs and a prompt to check the post description for the self-screen link.

ideas.title: Five common mouth findings that are not oral cancer
ideas.hook: Five things in your mouth that look worrying but probably aren't.
ideas.brief: The hook sets up relief rather than alarm, then the caption walks through each: frictional keratosis from a bitten cheek or ill-fitting denture, oral thrush that wipes away, lichen planus with its fine lacy lines on both cheeks, a burn from hot food that heals within days, and geographic tongue with its shifting pale-bordered patches. The closing line shifts the frame: the list isn't a reason to ignore changes, it's context for the one rule that matters, which is that anything new still present after two weeks deserves a look. Photo shows a close-up of lips or an open mouth in soft natural light. Caption closes with oralcheck.org/learn/white-and-red-patches.

ideas.title: Low-cost oral care options when you have no dentist
ideas.hook: When did you last have someone look inside your mouth?
ideas.brief: Slide 1 names the reader directly: this post is for anyone without a dentist, without insurance, or without money for a private appointment. Slide 2 lays out three options side by side: HRSA-funded community health centers that charge on a sliding scale, dental schools that offer lower-cost care, and free clinics that exist in many areas. Final slide: oralcheck.org/find-care searches all of them by location.

ideas.title: Gardasil 9 approved through age 45, most effective earlier
ideas.hook: The vaccine works best before exposure. It's still available after.
ideas.brief: The contrast between ideal timing and real-world eligibility is the spine of the post. The caption explains that Gardasil 9 protects against HPV-16 and HPV-18, the strains behind most HPV-related cancers, and that it's FDA-approved for ages 9 through 45. Adults who weren't vaccinated earlier may still benefit, and the caption notes that a doctor can advise on individual circumstances. One plain closing sentence clarifies what the vaccine cannot do: it can't treat an existing infection. Photo shows a young adult in a clinical setting, receiving a routine injection, candid rather than staged. Caption closes with oralcheck.org/learn/hpv.

ideas.title: Two white patches that look alike but are not the same
ideas.hook: Two patches in your mouth look almost identical.
ideas.brief: Slide 1 describes oral thrush: a yeast infection whose white coating wipes away, often leaving a red sore area underneath. Slide 2 describes leukoplakia: a patch that stays put when you try to rub it away. Slide 3 holds the line that matters for both: neither can be confirmed by eye, and any patch that is still there after two weeks gets checked. Final slide: oralcheck.org/learn/white-and-red-patches.

ideas.title: Leukoplakia: the white patch that cannot be scraped off
ideas.hook: A white patch you can rub off is one thing. One you cannot is another.
ideas.brief: Open on the contrast between a food residue or thrush that clears with rubbing and a leukoplakia that stays fixed to the tissue. Show the most common sites: the inner cheek, the tongue, and the floor of the mouth. Note that leukoplakia is usually painless, which is why it goes unnoticed for months, and that while most are benign, a share become malignant if left untreated. If a white patch will not come off and has no clear explanation, check it at oralcheck.org/learn/white-and-red-patches.

ideas.title: Mixed red-and-white speckled patches carry the highest risk
ideas.hook: A patch that is partly red, partly white carries more risk than either alone.
ideas.brief: Open on the contrast between a uniformly white patch and a speckled mix of red and white, naming the latter as the higher-risk type. Tour four sites in the mouth one at a time: the inner cheek (label: buccal mucosa), the tongue's lateral edge (label: lateral tongue), the floor of the mouth (label: floor of mouth), and the soft palate (label: soft palate), with one spoken line at each noting this is where speckled patches are found. Close on the defining rule: if it does not rub or scrape off, it needs a professional look. More at oralcheck.org/learn/white-and-red-patches.

ideas.title: Betel quid raises oral cancer risk with or without tobacco
ideas.hook: Tobacco-free doesn't mean risk-free. Not with betel quid.
ideas.brief: The contrast opens the post by challenging an assumption, then the caption grounds it in IARC's classification: betel quid, whether it contains tobacco or not, is a Group 1 carcinogen for oral cancer. That includes areca nut, paan and gutka. The closing line explains why the OralCheck screener asks about it specifically: the risk is independent of tobacco, so leaving it off a standard risk checklist would miss a meaningful exposure. Photo shows betel leaves and areca nut on a surface, or a market stall with paan ingredients. Caption closes with oralcheck.org/screener.

ideas.title: Survival rates for oral cancer by stage at detection
ideas.hook: Oral cancer caught while still localized has an 89% five-year survival rate.
ideas.brief: Slide 1 puts 89% at full size with one line of context: that is the five-year relative survival rate when oral cancer is found while it is still localized, according to SEER data. Slide 2 shows what changes as it spreads: about 70% once it reaches nearby tissue, about 36% once it has spread to distant sites. Slide 3 names what moves those numbers in the right direction: regular screening and not waiting on a sore or patch that does not heal, starting at oralcheck.org/learn/facts.

ideas.title: HPV exposure is common and most infections clear
ideas.hook: Have you ever thought about whether you've been exposed to HPV?
ideas.brief: A single calm sentence over a candid photo of two adults in conversation: 'Most sexually active adults have been exposed to HPV at some point, and the vast majority of infections clear on their own.' A second line notes that certain strains, particularly HPV-16, can drive DNA changes that lead to cancer in some people, which is why knowing your risk matters. Caption closes by directing viewers to oralcheck.org to take the free screener.

ideas.title: Reference card: oral cancer warning signs beyond colour
ideas.hook: Run your finger along the inside of one cheek.
ideas.brief: The card is laid out in plain document style, built to be saved. Three entries, each with a short label and a one-line description: irregular, raised, or hardened edges on a sore or patch; a sore that bleeds easily when touched; and a new lump or thickening in the cheek, tongue, gum, or floor of the mouth, often firm, like a pea under the skin. Footer line: any of these lasting more than two weeks gets checked at oralcheck.org/learn/signs.

ideas.title: Tobacco plus alcohol together multiply oral cancer risk
ideas.hook: Do you smoke and drink? The combined risk is not what you might expect.
ideas.brief: Open with the question framing the viewer's own habits, then move through three sites where tobacco and alcohol damage the same tissue together: the floor of the mouth (label: floor of mouth), the lateral tongue (label: lateral tongue), and the soft palate (label: soft palate). At each stop, one spoken line explains that both substances act on the same lining, and that alcohol may help tobacco carcinogens enter the cells. Close on the figure from the Hashibe 2009 pooled analysis: heavy smokers who also drink heavily face about 15 times the risk of people who do neither, and cutting back on either one brings that risk down. Run a free screen at oralcheck.org/learn/risk-factors.

ideas.title: HPV throat cancer at the base of tongue and tonsils
ideas.hook: You open wide, look in the mirror, and see nothing unusual.
ideas.brief: Start in that moment: the viewer has done what seems like a reasonable self-check and found nothing. Then explain that HPV-related cancers tend to start at the base of the tongue and the tonsils, an area called the oropharynx that sits too far back to see in a bathroom mirror. Because there is often no visible lesion and the site is hard to examine, these cancers are frequently caught later than cancers that appear on the lips or front of the tongue. Close with the practical step: a structured screener can flag the risk factors that a mirror cannot. Start at oralcheck.org/learn/hpv.

ideas.title: Median diagnosis age is 65, but the gap is narrowing
ideas.hook: 65 is the median age at diagnosis. It isn't the only age to watch.
ideas.brief: The figure and its limit occupy the same breath. The caption acknowledges that 65 is the SEER median, then immediately complicates it: HPV-related throat cancers are appearing more often in middle-aged adults, and age alone is no longer a reliable reason to dismiss a symptom. The post doesn't reframe 65 as irrelevant; it makes the case that a number is a midpoint, not a boundary. Photo shows a person in their forties or early fifties at a routine medical appointment, seated and attentive. Caption closes with oralcheck.org/learn/facts.

ideas.title: Red patch in your mouth: what it means
ideas.hook: Pull your cheek aside and look at the inner lining.
ideas.brief: Slide 1 opens with the physical instruction and names the reader directly: if you spot a flat red patch that has been there two weeks or more and does not hurt, this post is for you. Slide 2 introduces erythroplakia by plain description only, noting it is far less common than a white patch and easy to dismiss precisely because it is painless and undramatic. Slide 3 delivers the key fact: studies estimate 50% or more of red patches are already cancerous or precancerous at biopsy, making it the single most concerning thing you can find on your own. Final slide closes with a clear, calm instruction: if you found something that fits, do not wait for your next cleaning to mention it. Run a full self-check now at oralcheck.org.

ideas.title: 60,480 new oral cancer cases expected in the US this year
ideas.hook: How many Americans will be diagnosed with oral cancer this year?
ideas.brief: The question hangs for a beat before the caption answers it: an estimated 60,480 in 2026, according to SEER. The second sentence gives the other number without dressing it up: about 13,150 are expected to die of it. The closing line connects scale to action, noting that a free screener takes about two minutes and is the most concrete thing someone can do today. Photo shows a realistic crowd scene, a busy public space like a train station or market, to give the numbers a sense of physical scale without being graphic. Caption closes with oralcheck.org/learn/facts.

ideas.title: HPV-related oral cancer in men with no tobacco history
ideas.hook: You have never smoked. You assume that lowers your risk.
ideas.brief: Slide 1 sits with that assumption: for a long time, oral cancer was understood as a disease tied to tobacco, which made it easy to feel unaffected without that history. Slide 2 names the group most commonly diagnosed with HPV-related throat cancer: men between 40 and 60, most of them with no history of tobacco use. Slide 3 closes without alarm, just a prompt: knowing the full picture of risk is what makes early checking useful, at oralcheck.org/learn/hpv.

ideas.title: Two-minute oral self-exam you can do right now
ideas.hook: Get a mirror and find a light source.
ideas.brief: Each shot covers one area in the order a clinician would move through it: face and neck, lips, cheeks, gums, tongue top, tongue sides, tongue underside, floor of the mouth, roof of the mouth, then throat. On screen text for each shot names the area and tells the viewer exactly what to look for: anything new, a patch, a sore, a lump, or a colour change. The final frame holds on a plain slate: once a month, every month, oralcheck.org/learn/self-exam.

ideas.title: What the OralCheck screener can and cannot tell you
ideas.hook: A low score on the screener is not a clean bill of health.
ideas.brief: Slide 1 states the myth plainly: a low-risk result means you're fine. Slide 2 corrects it: the screener reads back the exposures you report, takes two minutes, needs no account, and never sees your mouth. It cannot tell you whether you have cancer. Slide 3 delivers the practical rule: if something in your mouth looks or feels wrong, that symptom means see a dentist regardless of your score. End card links to oralcheck.org/methods.

ideas.title: Where in your mouth would a tumour have room to hide?
ideas.hook: When did you last look at the inside of your cheek?
ideas.brief: The reel moves through four sites in the mouth, one spoken line and one label per shot: the floor of the mouth, the sides of the tongue, the cheek lining, and the tonsil area. At each stop, one sentence notes how visible that site is in a mirror. The closing line ties it together: only about 26% of oral cancers are found while still localized, and the rest have already reached nearby tissue by diagnosis. End card: oralcheck.org/learn/facts.

ideas.title: Risk factors you were born with still matter for screening
ideas.hook: Put your hand on your jaw for a moment.
ideas.brief: The image shows an older adult looking thoughtfully at their own reflection, cropped close on face and jaw. The question over the photo: 'Your age, sex and family history all affect your oral cancer risk. Are you adjusting what you can control to match?' The caption explains that these factors are fixed, but having several of them is a reason to be more careful about the ones that aren't, and to ask your dentist how often you should be screened. Closes with oralcheck.org/learn/prevention.

ideas.title: Self-check for the floor of your mouth under your tongue
ideas.hook: You're brushing your teeth and you notice something you haven't seen before.
ideas.brief: Shot 1: viewer is prompted to lift their tongue to the roof of their mouth. Shot 2: the camera labels the U-shaped tissue underneath as the floor of the mouth, noting it's one of the highest-risk sites. Shot 3: the viewer is guided to look at that tissue in a mirror while holding the position. The final line notes that a small tumour here can grow for months before causing any discomfort, which is why this check exists. Closes with oralcheck.org/learn/signs.

ideas.title: Every tobacco form raises oral cancer risk, not just cigarettes
ideas.hook: Switching to chewing tobacco is not a safer option for your mouth.
ideas.brief: The carousel is built as a saved-reference card. Slide 1 corrects the opening belief: the list covers every form, cigarettes, cigars, pipes, chewing tobacco, snuff and vaping products. Slide 2 states the proportion plainly: tobacco accounts for roughly 75% of traditional oral cavity cancers. Slide 3 adds the dose relationship: risk scales with how much and for how long. Final slide is a plain save-this card with the full list and oralcheck.org/learn/risk-factors.

ideas.title: Two-week rule: what heals and what does not
ideas.hook: A canker sore hurts and clears up. Oral cancer often does neither.
ideas.brief: The reel opens on that contrast, then names the warning sign: anything in the mouth that hasn't healed or gone away in two weeks. It then moves through the places that sign most often appears, the floor of the mouth, the sides of the tongue, the inner cheek, and the gumline, one spoken line per location. The closing note is practical: painless, persistent, bleeds easily, or simply unusual are all reasons to get it looked at. Closes with oralcheck.org/learn/signs.

ideas.title: Alcohol is a direct carcinogen in the mouth and risk rises with amount
ideas.hook: You pour a drink after work and don't give your mouth a second thought.
ideas.brief: The image shows a half-finished drink on a table, slightly out of focus, with a person's hand nearby. The single caption sentence reads: 'Alcohol is a direct carcinogen in the mouth, and the risk rises with how much and how often you drink.' The body of the caption adds the specific threshold: heavy drinking, more than three to four drinks a day, carries the highest risk, while keeping to moderate levels meaningfully lowers it compared to heavy use. Closes with oralcheck.org/learn/risk-factors.

ideas.title: What you're looking for during a monthly mouth self-exam
ideas.hook: You're standing at the bathroom mirror before bed with good light.
ideas.brief: Starting from that moment, the reel walks through one structure in detail: the floor of the mouth. It places it anatomically, describes what the tissue looks like when it's healthy, and says clearly what to watch for: a new patch, sore, lump, or change in colour that wasn't there last month. The final line pulls back to the broader habit: the full self-exam covers the same ground, once a month, and takes a couple of minutes. Closes with oralcheck.org/learn/self-exam.

ideas.title: Two differences between a canker sore and a cancer lesion
ideas.hook: Here are two things worth knowing before you decide to wait it out.
ideas.brief: The carousel is addressed precisely: slide 1 names the reader as someone who has a sore or patch in their mouth right now and isn't sure what it is. Slide 2 describes the canker sore: round or oval, white or yellow centre, red rim, painful, appears inside the mouth only, and heals on its own in 7 to 14 days. Slide 3 describes the oral cancer lesion: often painless early, irregular or raised edges, may bleed easily, does not heal. Slide 4 gives one instruction: if it's still there at two weeks, get it looked at, and links to oralcheck.org/learn/canker-sore-vs-oral-cancer.

ideas.title: Checking the sides of your tongue, the most common cancer site
ideas.hook: Stick your tongue out as far as it goes and look to your left.
ideas.brief: The reel opens on that instruction and holds there. The warning sign named is a persistent red or white patch, a sore, or a thickened area on the side or underside of the tongue. The reel then shows the two places it most often appears: the lateral border on each side, guiding the viewer to tilt their tongue and check each one. The final line is direct: the sides and underside are the most common site for oral cancer overall, and they're easy to miss without this check. Closes with oralcheck.org/learn/signs.

ideas.title: Men are diagnosed with oral cancer 2.6 times more than women
ideas.hook: 2.6 times. That's how much more often men are diagnosed with oral cancer than women.
ideas.brief: The image shows two men in conversation outdoors, candid and relaxed, mid-forties. The figure sits large over the photo. The caption unpacks what it means without alarm: the gap in incidence is real and consistent across SEER data, and HPV-related throat cancer in particular most often affects men aged 40 to 60, well before the median diagnosis age. The closing line is a direct prompt to check risk and closes with oralcheck.org/learn/facts.

ideas.title: Why a biopsy is the only way to know what a mouth patch is
ideas.hook: A patch looks harmless, so you decide to keep an eye on it.
ideas.brief: The reel corrects that instinct at the start: nobody can tell a harmless patch from a dangerous one by looking at it, not a clinician, not a photograph. It then walks the viewer through what a biopsy actually is, one step per shot: a short appointment, a small sample taken under local anaesthetic, and a look at that sample under a microscope. The final shot makes the size of it plain: it's the only thing that turns a worry into an answer. Closes with oralcheck.org/learn/white-and-red-patches.

ideas.title: White patch that wipes away versus one that stays put
ideas.hook: One white patch rubs off. The other one doesn't. That difference matters.
ideas.brief: Slide 1 opens on that contrast and asks the reader one question: have you ever noticed a white patch in your mouth and tried to rub it away? Slide 2 explains that oral thrush, a yeast infection, wipes away and often leaves a red sore area underneath. Slide 3 explains that a leukoplakia patch stays put when rubbed. Slide 4 delivers the shared rule: neither can be confirmed by eye, and any patch that persists for two weeks gets checked by a dentist. Closes with oralcheck.org/learn/white-and-red-patches.

ideas.title: How oral cancer risk changes after quitting tobacco
ideas.hook: Have you used tobacco in the past, even if you stopped years ago?
ideas.brief: The reel moves through three moments in a quitting timeline, one spoken line and one label per shot. First stop: active use, where tobacco is the single biggest modifiable risk factor for oral cancer. Second stop: a few years after quitting, where risk has already dropped measurably. Third stop: long-term ex-users, where risk approaches that of people who never used tobacco. The closing line is plain: it's never too late for it to count. Closes with oralcheck.org/learn/prevention.

ideas.title: Median oral cancer diagnosis age is 65, with one important caveat
ideas.hook: The median age at oral cancer diagnosis is 65.
ideas.brief: The image shows an adult in their mid-forties at a routine health appointment, seated and calm. The caption carries the fact forward without alarm: HPV-related throat cancers are appearing more often in middle-aged adults, so age alone isn't a reason to dismiss a symptom or skip a check. The closing line is direct: if something in your mouth hasn't healed in two weeks, it's worth getting looked at regardless of how old you are. Closes with oralcheck.org/learn/facts.

ideas.title: Gum cancer can look exactly like gum disease
ideas.hook: Sore, receding gums usually mean gum disease. Not always.
ideas.brief: The reel opens on that correction, then moves into a close look at the gumline: where it sits, what healthy gum tissue looks like, and what warrants attention. The key clue named on screen is teeth that have become loose without a clear dental cause. The final line is calm and specific: gum cancer can mimic gum disease closely enough that people wait, so anything that isn't responding to treatment or doesn't have an explanation should be mentioned to a dentist. Closes with oralcheck.org/learn/signs.

ideas.title: What your dentist checks for during a routine visit
ideas.hook: Open your mouth and tilt toward the light.
ideas.brief: Slide 1 opens with the instruction and names the six sites a dentist examines: lips, gums, tongue, cheeks, palate, throat. Slide 2 explains that most early-stage oral cancers are found during exactly this kind of routine check, and that the exam takes only a minute or two. Slide 3 notes that people who skip dental care are more likely to have cancer caught at a later stage, when outcomes are worse, and directs viewers to oralcheck.org/learn/prevention to learn what to watch for between visits.

ideas.title: HPV throat cancer starts where you can't see it
ideas.hook: HPV-related cancers tend to start at the base of the tongue.
ideas.brief: The reel opens on a simple anatomical diagram or close-up illustration of the oropharynx, with a voiceover naming the two sites: the base of the tongue and the tonsils. A second beat explains that there is often no visible lesion in a mirror, so self-checks can miss these entirely. The reel closes on the reason this matters: because the area is out of sight, these cancers are frequently caught later than others, and a dentist or clinician is the right person to examine it. CTA directs to oralcheck.org/learn/hpv.

ideas.title: White patch in your mouth that won't scrape off
ideas.hook: Have you ever noticed a white patch inside your mouth?
ideas.brief: A single real close-up photo of the inside of a mouth, with the question set in clean type over it. The caption explains that leukoplakia is a white patch that can't be scraped off and isn't explained by anything obvious, and that it's usually painless, which is why it goes unnoticed for months. It notes that most are benign but that a share can become malignant if left untreated, and closes with a prompt to visit oralcheck.org/learn/white-and-red-patches if a patch has been present for more than two weeks.

ideas.title: Painless neck lump as a first sign of throat cancer
ideas.hook: Have you felt a lump in your neck that wasn't there before?
ideas.brief: The reel uses a tour format with three labeled stops. Stop one: the neck, with a spoken line explaining that a painless lump there is often the first visible sign of HPV-related throat cancer, caused by lymph node involvement. Stop two: the tonsils, noting this is where many of these cancers begin, often without any surface lesion. Stop three: the throat, with the closing line that a swollen neck node lasting more than two weeks without an obvious infection is worth getting checked. CTA points to oralcheck.org/learn/hpv.

ideas.title: HPV overtook tobacco as the top cause of throat cancer
ideas.hook: HPV is now the leading cause of oropharyngeal cancers in the US.
ideas.brief: Slide 1 carries the headline figure: HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancers rose 225% from 1988 to 2004, while HPV-negative ones fell by half (Chaturvedi et al., 2011). Slide 2 adds the geographic precision: this shift applies to the oropharynx, the tonsils, base of tongue and back of the throat, and tobacco remains the dominant driver of cancers in the mouth itself. Slide 3 addresses what to do with this information, directing viewers to oralcheck.org/learn/hpv to understand their own risk factors and to take the free screener.

ideas.title: Speckled red-and-white patch carries the highest risk
ideas.hook: A red patch and a white patch don't carry the same risk.
ideas.brief: The reel opens on that contrast and then focuses on the one type that sits above both: the mixed red-and-white speckled patch, which carries the highest malignant potential of any patch type. A second beat introduces the single most important physical test: if it doesn't rub or scrape off, it needs professional assessment. The reel closes by naming the places these patches most often appear, the tongue, the floor of the mouth and the inside of the cheeks, and directs viewers to oralcheck.org/learn/white-and-red-patches.

ideas.title: Irregular edges and a sore that bleeds when touched
ideas.hook: Some warning signs are about texture and shape, not colour.
ideas.brief: A single real close-up photo anchors the post, showing the inside of a mouth in a way that makes texture visible. The caption names three physical signs in plain language: irregular, raised or hardened edges on a sore; a sore that bleeds easily when touched; and a new lump or thickening in the cheek, tongue, gum or floor of the mouth that feels firm, like a pea under the skin. It closes by directing viewers to oralcheck.org/learn/signs if any of these has been present for two weeks or more.

ideas.title: No pain doesn't mean no problem in early oral cancer
ideas.hook: You notice a small pale patch on the inside of your cheek.
ideas.brief: The reel opens in second person: the patch has been there a few weeks, it doesn't hurt, so it hasn't felt urgent. A second beat names the warning signs that most often appear without pain: red patches, white patches and early ulcers, and walks through the places they tend to show up, the tongue, the cheeks, the floor of the mouth. The closing beat explains that pain, when it does arrive, often signals nerve involvement or ulceration and a later stage, which is exactly why the two-week rule exists. CTA points to oralcheck.org/learn/signs.

ideas.title: How tobacco and alcohol multiply risk when used together
ideas.hook: Press one finger to your lower lip and hold it there.
ideas.brief: Slide 1 uses that opening gesture to anchor the reader in the mouth itself, then introduces the core fact: tobacco and alcohol together don't add their risks, they multiply them. Slide 2 puts the specific finding in frame: people who smoke more than a pack a day and drink three or more drinks a day carry about 15 times the oral cancer risk of people who do neither, from a pooled analysis of 17 studies (Hashibe 2009), and explains that alcohol may help tobacco carcinogens cross into the cells lining the mouth. Slide 3 closes with the most actionable point: cutting back on either one, not necessarily both, significantly lowers risk, with a CTA to oralcheck.org/learn/risk-factors.

ideas.title: Betel quid raises oral cancer risk even without tobacco
ideas.hook: Paan without tobacco is safer for your mouth. It isn't.
ideas.brief: The reel opens by naming that belief plainly and correcting it: betel quid, areca nut, paan and gutka are all classified as Group 1 carcinogens for oral cancer by the WHO's cancer agency (IARC), regardless of whether tobacco is added. A tour of three labeled sites follows: the cheek lining where the quid typically sits, the floor of the mouth and the gums, each with a spoken line about what changes to look for. The reel closes by noting that the OralCheck screener asks about betel quid use specifically for this reason, and directs viewers to oralcheck.org/screener.

ideas.title: Where to find low-cost oral cancer screening near you
ideas.hook: Type your zip code into the search bar at oralcheck.org/find-care.
ideas.brief: A real photo of a community health clinic or dental school setting anchors the post, showing a patient in a chair rather than a clinical setup. The caption opens by naming the instruction directly, then explains what comes back: HRSA-funded community health centers that charge on a sliding scale, dental schools offering lower-cost care, and free clinics in many areas. It closes by affirming that not having a dentist or insurance isn't a reason to skip a check, and that the tool at oralcheck.org/find-care is free to use.

ideas.title: 60,480 diagnoses and 13,150 deaths: the 2026 US numbers
ideas.hook: Put your tongue to the roof of your mouth and hold it.
ideas.brief: The reel opens with that physical anchor, then moves through a tour of four labeled sites with a figure attached to each stop to build toward the full picture. Stop one: the lips and oral cavity, described as the most visible sites. Stop two: the base of the tongue and tonsils, the oropharynx. Stop three: the throat and pharynx. Stop four: the full count, 60,480 Americans expected to be diagnosed in 2026 and about 13,150 expected to die of it, per SEER estimates. The closing line is plain: knowing what to look for is the first step, and the OralCheck screener at oralcheck.org/learn/facts is free.
